techniques.name: Platt Scaling
techniques.description: Platt scaling turns a classifier's raw scores into calibrated probabilities, meaning that among the cases given a probability of 0.3, about 30 per cent turn out to be positive. It was introduced for support vector machines, whose outputs are distances from a decision boundary rather than probabilities, and applies to any binary classifier that produces a real-valued score. After the classifier is trained, a two-parameter logistic (sigmoid) curve, P(y = 1 | f) = 1 / (1 + exp(A·f + B)), is fitted by maximum likelihood to map each score f to a probability, using labelled cases the classifier was not trained on, taken from a held-out set or from cross-validation folds. The fitted curve is strictly monotonic, so the order of cases and ranking measures such as the area under the ROC curve are unchanged; only the probability attached to each case moves. The output is a recalibrated model, assessed with a reliability diagram (predicted probability plotted against observed frequency) and the Brier score or log loss before and after.

example_use_cases.description: A retail bank's credit-risk team finds that its gradient-boosted default model ranks applicants well but squeezes predicted default probabilities towards the middle of the range. Before the probabilities feed expected-loss provisioning, the team fits Platt scaling on a held-out year of loan outcomes and checks on a reliability diagram that predicted and observed default rates agree in every score decile.

A benefits agency uses a linear support vector machine to flag claims for manual review, but its margin scores mean nothing to caseworkers. The team applies Platt scaling so the review screen can show the probability that a claim needs correcting, publishes the calibration curve in the caseworker guidance, and explains that the figure is a rate across similar claims rather than a verdict on the individual.

A hospital network recalibrates a deployed malnutrition-risk model by fitting a two-parameter logistic map to the model's log-odds on recent admissions, then compares calibration intercept and slope separately for Black and White patients and for men and women, to check that the same risk score means the same likelihood of malnutrition in each group before the scores guide dietitian referrals.

limitations.description: The sigmoid shape is an assumption. It corrects the S-shaped distortion typical of support vector machines and boosted trees, whose probabilities bunch towards the middle, but not the reverse distortion of overconfident models such as naive Bayes, whose probabilities pile up near 0 and 1. Where the reliability diagram shows that pattern, a flexible method such as isotonic regression is needed.

It works best when the classifier's scores for the two classes are spread in a similar way (roughly normal with equal variance). In highly imbalanced problems this often fails, and a two-parameter fit can leave the rare class poorly calibrated, which an overall score such as the Brier score can hide.

The curve must be fitted on labelled cases that played no part in training. The classifier separates its own training data better than new data, so a curve fitted to training scores overstates confidence in use; the cost is a held-out calibration set taken from scarce labelled data, or cross-validation with several model fits.

A single curve fitted across the whole population does not guarantee calibration within each subgroup. Fitting a separate curve per group needs group membership at prediction time, which may be unavailable or unlawful to use, and enough labelled cases in every group to estimate two parameters reliably.

It is defined for two classes. For multiclass problems each class is calibrated against the rest and the resulting probabilities are renormalised to sum to one, adding two parameters per class; for multiclass neural networks, temperature scaling, which fits one parameter shared by all classes, is the simpler alternative.

techniques.name: Machine Unlearning
techniques.description: Machine unlearning enables removal of specific training data's influence from trained models without complete retraining. This technique addresses privacy rights like GDPR's right to be forgotten by selectively erasing learned patterns associated with particular data points, individuals, or sensitive attributes. Methods include exact unlearning (provably equivalent to retraining without the data), approximate unlearning (efficient algorithms that closely approximate retraining), and certified unlearning (providing formal guarantees about information removal).

example_use_cases.description: Responding to user deletion requests in a social media recommendation system by removing all influence of that user's historical interactions, ensuring GDPR compliance and verifiable data removal.

Enabling a financial institution to demonstrate regulatory compliance by providing cryptographic proof that a former customer's transaction history has been completely removed from credit risk assessment models following account closure.

limitations.description: Exact unlearning for complex models like deep neural networks is computationally expensive, often nearly as costly as full retraining.
Approximate unlearning methods may not provide strong guarantees that information has been fully removed, potentially leaving residual influence.
Difficult to verify unlearning effectiveness, as adversaries might extract information about supposedly removed data through membership inference or other attacks.
Repeated unlearning requests can degrade model performance significantly, especially if many data points are removed from the training distribution.
Requires access to model architecture and training process details (white-box access), making it difficult to apply to third-party models or models where internal structure is proprietary.
Particularly challenging for very large foundation models where even storing checkpoints for potential retraining is infeasible, limiting practical applicability to smaller, domain-specific models.

techniques.name: Isotonic Regression Calibration
techniques.description: Isotonic regression calibration turns a classifier's scores into calibrated probabilities by fitting a step-shaped function that never decreases as the score rises. Unlike a fixed curve, it assumes nothing about the shape of the miscalibration except that a higher score should never mean a lower chance of the positive outcome, so it can correct any distortion that leaves the cases in the right order. It is fitted on labelled cases the classifier was not trained on: the cases are sorted by score, and the pool-adjacent-violators algorithm repeatedly merges neighbouring groups whose observed positive rates are out of order, until the rates rise steadily with the score. Each merged group's observed rate becomes the calibrated probability for scores in its range, and the result is assessed with a reliability diagram (predicted probability plotted against observed frequency) and the Brier score before and after.

example_use_cases.description: A clinical research team builds a random forest on electronic health records to predict which adolescents will attempt suicide. The forest ranks patients well, but its vote shares are not probabilities, so the team fits isotonic regression on held-out records and reports calibration slope, intercept and Brier score before the risk estimates are used to prioritise clinical follow-up.

An insurer's pricing team applies isotonic recalibration to the output of its claim-probability model, fitted on a large portfolio, so that within each band of predicted risk the average prediction equals the observed claim rate on the calibration data and no group of policyholders systematically subsidises another.

An online marketplace scores listings for fraud with a naive Bayes text classifier whose probabilities cluster near 0 and 1, and analysts had been treating them as near-certainties. With tens of thousands of labelled past cases available, the team fits isotonic calibration so the review queue shows probabilities that match observed fraud rates, and shares the reliability diagram with the analysts.

limitations.description: It needs plenty of calibration data. With fewer than about a thousand labelled cases the step function follows noise in the calibration set, and the two-parameter curve of Platt scaling usually does as well or better; isotonic regression pays off when calibration data are plentiful.

The output is a step function, so many different scores receive exactly the same probability. These ties discard distinctions the model made within a step, can change ranking measures such as the area under the ROC curve after calibration, and matter when a decision threshold falls inside a wide step.

It relies on the classifier's ordering being right: a higher score must never mean a lower chance of the outcome. Where the model ranks cases wrongly over some range of scores, isotonic regression cannot repair the ranking and instead flattens that range into a single probability.

Probabilities at the extremes rest on little data. The outermost steps can be fitted from a handful of cases and may sit at or near 0 or 1, and common implementations clip scores beyond the range seen in calibration to the end values, so the most extreme predictions are the least trustworthy.
